items.q: In toxicology, what does LD50 mean?
options: The dose that kills half of a test population
The dose at which half the test animals first show any effect
The dose that kills 50 animals out of a test group
The largest dose that causes no deaths in the test

why.correct: LD50 is the lethal dose for 50% of a test population, usually in milligrams of substance per kilogram of body mass.
options: Right: LD stands for lethal dose, and 50 for the 50% of test animals it kills.
A dose that causes any effect in half the animals is a different measure; LD50 counts deaths only.
The 50 is a percent of the group, not a count of animals, so it works for a group of any size.
That would be a safe-looking dose with zero deaths, not the dose that kills half the animals.

items.q: Pesticide P has an LD50 of 20 mg/kg in rats. Pesticide Q has an LD50 of 2,000 mg/kg in rats. Which statement is correct?
options: Q is more toxic, because its LD50 is the larger number
P is more toxic: less of it per kilogram kills half the rats
P and Q are equally toxic, since both were tested on rats
Q is safe for people, since its LD50 is above 1,000 mg/kg

why.correct: LD50 and toxicity run in opposite directions: the lower the LD50, the more toxic the substance. P is $\frac{2{,}000}{20} = 100$ times as toxic as Q per kilogram.
options: A larger LD50 means more of the substance is needed to kill half the rats, so Q is less toxic.
Right: a lower LD50 means less of the substance is needed to kill, so it is more toxic.
Testing in the same species makes them comparable, but the LD50s differ a hundredfold.
A high LD50 means low toxicity in rats, not that a substance is safe; large doses can still kill.

items.q: The LD50 of a pesticide in rats is 60 mg/kg. What dose of pesticide would be expected to kill half of a group of rats that each have a mass of 0.40 kg? Give the dose for one rat in milligrams.

why.correct: The setup multiplies the dose per kilogram by the body mass, so kilograms cancel: $60\,\frac{\text{mg}}{\text{kg}} \times 0.40\,\text{kg} = 24\,\text{mg}$.

mistakes.why: You divided the LD50 by the body mass. LD50 is milligrams for each kilogram, so multiply: 60 mg/kg × 0.40 kg = 24 mg.
60 is the dose for each kilogram of rat. A 0.40 kg rat needs only 0.40 of that: 60 mg/kg × 0.40 kg.

items.q: A cleaning chemical has an LD50 of 25 mg/kg, measured in dogs. Write the setup, with units, for the dose expected to kill half of a group of 12 kg dogs, then give the answer in milligrams.

why.correct: Multiply the LD50 by the body mass so kilograms cancel: $25\,\frac{\text{mg}}{\text{kg}} \times 12\,\text{kg} = 300\,\text{mg}$.

mistakes.why: Dividing by the body mass leaves mg/kg² and a dose that shrinks as the dog gets bigger. Multiply by the mass so the kilograms cancel.
The body mass divided by the LD50 has no meaning here. Start from the LD50 and multiply by the mass: 25 mg/kg × 12 kg.
0.3 is the dose in grams. The question asks for milligrams: 25 mg/kg × 12 kg = 300 mg.

items.q: A solvent has an LD50 of 500 mg/kg in rats. If people reacted the same way (a big assumption), what dose would be expected to kill half of a group of 80 kg adults? Give the answer in grams.

why.correct: First the dose in milligrams: $500\,\frac{\text{mg}}{\text{kg}} \times 80\,\text{kg} = 40{,}000\,\text{mg}$. Then grams: $40{,}000\,\text{mg} \times \frac{1\,\text{g}}{1{,}000\,\text{mg}} = 40\,\text{g}$. Rat data only estimate the human value.

mistakes.why: 40,000 is the dose in milligrams. Divide by 1,000 to change milligrams to grams: 40,000 mg ÷ 1,000 mg/g = 40 g.
You divided the LD50 by the body mass. Multiply instead: 500 mg/kg × 80 kg = 40,000 mg, which is 40 g.

items.q: Why is LD50 reported in milligrams per kilogram of body mass instead of in milligrams alone?
options: Milligrams alone would be too small a unit to measure a lethal dose in large animals
Big animals need bigger doses, so per-kilogram values compare fairly
Kilograms are the unit of the substance and milligrams the unit of the animal
Per-kilogram values show how long the substance stays in the body

why.correct: A dose spread through a bigger body is more dilute, so the same milligrams harm a large animal less. Dividing by body mass puts every test on one scale.
options: Milligrams are fine for measuring doses; the reason is fairness across body sizes.
Right: dividing by body mass lets a mouse, a rat and a dog be compared on one scale.
It is the other way around: milligrams of substance for each kilogram of animal.
How long a substance stays in the body is a separate question that LD50 does not measure.

items.q: US pesticide labels group products by how toxic they are when swallowed. Products with an oral LD50 of 50 mg/kg or less carry the signal word DANGER; above 50 to 500 mg/kg, WARNING; above 500 to 5,000 mg/kg, CAUTION; above 5,000 mg/kg, no signal word is required. A new insecticide has an oral LD50 of 30 mg/kg in rats. Which label should it carry, and why?
options: CAUTION, because 30 mg/kg is a small number
WARNING, because 30 mg/kg falls between 50 and 500
DANGER, because 30 mg/kg is in the most toxic group
No signal word, because rats are not people

why.correct: The lower the LD50, the stronger the warning: 30 mg/kg is in the 50 mg/kg or less group, labeled DANGER (EPA toxicity category I).
options: A small LD50 means high toxicity, so it belongs in the most toxic group, not the least.
30 is below 50, so it does not fall in the above 50 to 500 mg/kg group.
Right: 30 mg/kg is at or below 50 mg/kg, the most toxic group.
Labels are set from animal tests like this one; a rat LD50 of 30 mg/kg puts it in the top group.

items.q: Which list orders the chemicals from most toxic to least toxic?
options: D, C, B, A
B, A, D, C
C, D, A, B
A, B, C, D

why.correct: Most toxic means the smallest dose kills half the rats: A (4), B (40), C (320), D (4,000 mg/kg).
options: This lists them from largest LD50 to smallest, which is least toxic to most toxic.
This order does not follow the LD50 values at all. Sort by LD50, smallest first.
This order mixes high and low values. The smallest LD50 marks the most toxic chemical.
Right: toxicity falls as LD50 rises, so the smallest LD50 (A, 4 mg/kg) is the most toxic.

items.q: How many times as toxic as chemical D is chemical A, per kilogram of body mass?

why.correct: Half the rats die at 4 mg/kg of A but at 4,000 mg/kg of D, so A is $\frac{4{,}000}{4} = 1{,}000$ times as toxic.

mistakes.why: You divided the smaller LD50 by the larger. Toxicity is the inverse of LD50, so divide D’s LD50 by A’s: 4,000 ÷ 4.
A difference does not say how many times as toxic. Divide the LD50s: 4,000 mg/kg ÷ 4 mg/kg = 1,000.

items.q: Write the setup, with units, for the dose of chemical C expected to kill half of a group of 0.30 kg rats, then give the answer in milligrams.

mistakes.why: Dividing by the mass gives mg/kg², not milligrams. Multiply the LD50 by the body mass so kilograms cancel.
The rat is 0.30 kg, not 30 kg. Use the mass in kilograms, since the LD50 is per kilogram.
You used 30 kg instead of 0.30 kg. The rats have a mass of 0.30 kg: 320 mg/kg × 0.30 kg = 96 mg.

items.q: Which conclusion do the data support?
options: Chemical D is the most toxic, since it has the largest LD50
Chemical A is harmless to people, since the tests used rats
Chemical B reaches its LD50 at one eighth of the dose of C
Chemical C kills 320 out of each 1,000 rats that swallow a dose of it

why.correct: The table gives doses, not counts of deaths. Comparing LD50s by division shows how many times as toxic one chemical is.
options: The largest LD50 means the most substance is needed to kill, so D is the least toxic.
A is the most toxic chemical in rats; rat tests suggest risk to people, not safety.
Right: $\frac{320}{40} = 8$, so B reaches the LD50 at one eighth of C’s dose.
The 320 is a dose in mg/kg, not a count of deaths. At that dose half the rats die.

items.q: Read the graph. What is the LD50 of the solvent in mice?

why.correct: Go across from 50% on the vertical axis to the line, then down to the dose axis: the LD50 is 400 mg/kg.

mistakes.why: 50 is the percent on the vertical axis. LD50 is the dose on the horizontal axis where the line crosses 50% of mice killed.
At 300 mg/kg only 30% of the mice died. Move up to 50% on the vertical axis, then across to the line and down.

items.q: What percent of the mice died at a dose of 600 mg/kg?

why.correct: Read straight up from 600 mg/kg to the line, then across: 84% of the mice died.
options: Right: the point at 600 mg/kg sits at 84% of mice killed.
68% is the value at 500 mg/kg. Read straight up from 600 mg/kg.
96% is the value at 800 mg/kg, the highest dose tested.
50% is the response at the LD50 (400 mg/kg), not at 600 mg/kg.

items.q: A mouse has a mass of 0.025 kg. Using the LD50 you read from the graph, what dose of the solvent, in milligrams, would be expected to kill half of a group of such mice?

mistakes.why: You divided the LD50 by the body mass. Multiply instead, so kilograms cancel: 400 mg/kg × 0.025 kg = 10 mg.
400 is the dose for each kilogram. A mouse has a mass of only 0.025 kg: 400 mg/kg × 0.025 kg.

items.q: Each dose in the study was given to a group of 50 mice, not to one mouse. Why?
options: A group of 50 lets the researchers use a smaller dose for each mouse
Mice live in groups, so a single mouse would not eat the solvent
Mice vary, so the percent of a group shows the typical response
Larger groups make the solvent more toxic to each mouse

why.correct: Replication: individuals vary, so the LD50 is read from the percent of a group that dies at each dose.
options: The dose per kilogram is set by the design, not by how many mice are in the group.
The dose is given directly; the reason for groups is that individuals vary.
Right: one animal might be unusually tough or weak; a group averages that out.
Group size does not change how toxic the solvent is to any one animal.

items.q: Build a testable hypothesis for the mouse study in the graph.

why.correct: A hypothesis is a statement with a direction: the dose is what changes and the percent killed is what is measured.

specific.frame: If the ___, then the ___ will ___, because ___.

change.label: Change
options: dose of solvent increases
number of mice in each group increases
color of the solvent changes

why.1: Group size is kept the same; the study changes the dose.
why.2: Color is not what the study changes or measures.

dv.label: What is measured
options: percent of mice killed
mass of each mouse
LD50 of the solvent

why.1: Body mass is kept similar; deaths are what the graph shows.
why.2: The LD50 is read from the results; it is one number, not what changes with dose.

direction.label: Direction
options: increase
decrease
change

why.1: Higher doses kill more mice in the graph, so deaths rise.
why.2: "Change" gives no direction; a hypothesis says which way.

specific.model: If the dose of solvent increases, then the percent of mice killed will increase, because a larger dose per kilogram does more damage to body tissues.
